size.note: Newman's Birds gives 18–21 cm, and 60 cm for the breeding male.

habitat: Small flocks, mainly in thornveld. It parasitises the Green-winged Pytilia.
summary: A common resident. The breeding male has a creamy-buff nape and underparts, a rufous breast, and tapering tail feathers. It differs from the Broad-tailed Paradise Whydah in those tapering feathers. The female and non-breeding male have bolder black-and-white head stripes than the Pin-tailed Whydah. The song is short and sparrow-like, with an occasional 'chit'. The Kemp name Paradise Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: The Pin-tailed Whydah is pied, and its female has less bold head stripes.

underparts.pattern: Creamy-buff underparts and a rufous breast.

head.pattern: Bolder black-and-white head stripes than the Pin-tailed Whydah. The non-breeding male is similar.

viewNotes.note: Creamy-buff nape and underparts, a rufous breast, and a tapering tail.
In display the two short tail feathers are held erect. He also hovers, and the tail undulates.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: A short sparrow-like song, and an occasional 'chit'. No South African grade A recording was found. The grade A song is from Awash National Park in Ethiopia. The filename is XC209990-Eastern Paradise-Whydah2014-12-25-1.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common resident, and Avibase lists Eastern Paradise-Whydah without marking it rare, so all twelve months are listed. The stored name remains Long-tailed Paradise Whydah. The stored length covers 18–21 cm and the 60 cm breeding male. No South African grade A recording was found, so the Ethiopian grade A song is used. The Kemp name Paradise Whydah and the code RB were left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^13=8192 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 4096–16384.
